utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT- 04-83-PT, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the parties make their appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. Geoff Roberts, my legal assistant, I appear today on behalf of General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. You are quite recently appointed as permanent counsel. I'd like to say, welcome on board.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see there are many issues today. There are no outstanding motions, so let me deal directly with the disclosure matter. My understanding is that 66(A)(1) disclosure is complete with the caveat that former duty counsel hasn't reviewed the documents but the Accused himself received the statements, all the documents, and the 30 days period during which the Defence can file a preliminary motion started only as of the date of the assignment of the permanent counsel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And a little addition to that in that this morning we met with Defence, and they, too, were served with the supporting material. So that's in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was informed by our Chamber's Senior Legal Officer that Prosecution raised a possibility of amending the indictment during the 65 ter meeting last week. Do you have any comment on that? In particular, I'd like to know what the amendment would look like, whether it is an addition or some replacement of counts or restructuring this legal basis. Yes, please, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution in its investigation of this case was looking at a number of different crime bases. As Your Honour appreciates, given that the Accused is the former commander of the ABiH and in a relatively senior position, there were a large number of potential crime bases that we were investigating. There are still approximately three of those crime bases that we are interested in with respect to this Accused. So the short answer to Your Honour's question is that we would be looking to add three additional crime bases to the indictment as it currently exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In addition to the current charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We are not looking to replace any of the existing crime base but, in fact, to add three additional crime bases to the indictment as it currently stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But when do you think the Prosecution could file the amendment, actually leave to amend the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would anticipate, Your Honour, that we would be in a position to seek leave to amend the indictment no later than the end of October 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be about around four months time from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it not be done a bit earlier? By the end of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I assure you, Your Honour, that we are working as quickly as possible. It might be possible, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you set an aim date by the end of September, and if necessary, you can ask for an extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed on that basis. 66(A)(2) disclosure. I was informed that you anticipate about 50 or 60 witnesses as the indictment stands, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think you can complete the disclosure, together with expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as my colleague just indicated, this is a very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Apart from the amendment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a bit premature to give a specific time period because of the fact, as my colleague indicated before, the seniority of the Accused, we are still in doing some investigations ongoing. And so I think it may be a little premature at this stage for us to be able to give an exact, period and that is why I think we said maybe 50 to 60 witnesses because we are still assessing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which means you can disclose these materials on an ongoing basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's precisely what I said. We are disclosing as an ongoing basis, but as to say when completion -- to give a date for completion, it's a bit difficult at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber, as well as myself, wish to have this case be ready for trial as soon as possible. So I'd like to have -- very much to have an aim date for -- but it may be a bit too early but roughly. Can it not be done in three months' time from now? Is it too early?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I was just suggesting that to my colleague, maybe in terms of three to four months, I would think. Probably the end of October -- possibly the end of September, October. Let's have it the end of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's endeavour to have it completed by the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together -- and how many expert witnesses? Three, I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any problem or issues in relation to Rule 68 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No. This is an ongoing process. The translations have been sent on to ISS, and that's been ongoing, and we have created the folders for the Defence for EDS, and that is in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When reading the transcript of 65 ter conference, I read -- a Delic directory? You create a special directory for the purpose of specific Accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not the case that you allow access to entire material, which is called EDS to the Accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That is it, EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: EDS. And what's different? EDS contains every material.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: All the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even not related to the Delic case. You create a specific EDS for every case?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Each individual Accused has -- and Defence have their own EDS directory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it should be the Prosecution who makes the first search programme, first off, at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it due to a word in the rules? Because -- what's the -- 68(2) or (B)? Is it because the Rule 68(2) says the Prosecutor shall make available to the Defence collections of relevant material?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: All relevant material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's because of that word.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, by your leave, I would just like to briefly add something to the questions that you have now been discussing with the Prosecutor. Firstly, I received the supporting materials to the indictment, and just for the record I would like to state something. The material so far received by the Accused also comprised certain documents that were not originally seen by the judge who confirmed the indictment. I wish to state for the record that we do not consider this to be proper supporting material since it was never confirmed by the relevant judge. Secondly, the materials received by the accused, bearing in mind the fact that he was not sufficiently qualified to go through these documents, we might now be able to say that there are certain drawbacks to this material, certain parts missing, whole sections of various transcripts, indicating certain statements. I just want the record to reflect this. I will be asking the Prosecutor to have a discussion about this later on. What we believe is particularly relevant at this point in time is the application of Rule 68. It is obviously the position of the Prosecutor that the materials available on EDS that the Defence now has access to need not be served to the Defence pursuant to the rule on disclosure. I believe the fact that there are materials available on EDS does not absolve the Prosecutor from their duty to deliver these materials to us pursuant to Rule 68. I have a lot of experience with EDS, and based Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on this experience I can say these materials are sometimes exceedingly difficult to access. There is an enormous amount of these documents. I've not checked whether there is a special directory for the Delic case; I certainly didn't see that there was. At any rate, I remain adamant that we be given these documents, as well as any other materials related to Rule 68. Something else I realised when I read the transcript from the 65 ter conference: The Prosecutor is familiar with the material from the Hadzihasanovic case. They are exceedingly familiar with the evidence in that case. I've been monitoring this case on a sporadic basis, and I notice there was a lot of 68 Rule material being used. Needless to say, we shall search every database that we have access to, but we believe that among those documents there were documents that were delivered to the OTP pursuant to Rule 70. Be that as it may, we remain adamant that exhibits should be delivered to us as soon as possible, pursuant to Rule 68. I was very surprised when I read that the Prosecutor had referred to four specific documents under Rule 68. I am positive that they have a lot more in their possession, a lot more exhibits in their possession pursuant to Rule 68. What I have managed to do in these days since I was appointed, I got in touch with the relevant archives, the relevant state archives in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was informed that since 2003 the Prosecutor have had in their possession a lot of documents, and this group of documents includes documents under Rule 68. Even if these documents had not yet been translated into English, I believe that the OTP now have a lot of people in their teams who know the Bosnian language, and they should start translating these documents. It may seem now that we have a lot of time on our hands to prepare our Defence, but as we all know, time flies, and I think these documents should be delivered as soon as possible. Finally, concerning the fact that the OTP appears to have certain amendments to the indictment in store, I believe we shall be filing our own motion concerning any amendments, and we shall not wait for mid- October or even late October to file this motion. Rather, we shall be filing the motion before that time. That's all I have for the time being. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. There are some parts I didn't follow. When you said that there are four statements, what are they?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure how this has been interpreted. In actual fact, what I said was that there were certain testimonies that the Prosecutor referred to in the annex to the documents they have delivered. These are not complete testimonies; these are just excerpts. I will talk to the OTP about this, and I will ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Are they part of supporting materials?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The documents that we referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I'm speaking about is the fact that the OTP served on the Accused excerpts from a number of testimonies instead of complete testimonies. But this is something that I can discuss with the OTP after this status conference; I don't think we should be going into further into that issue now. Further, there is one document that seems to be missing in its entirety. So much for the supporting material. As for exculpatory material, I've referred to four documents. At the 65 ter Rule conference the OTP mentioned as few as four documents, which they believe they are in their possession. They believe these are Rule 68 documents, and this is something that worries me since I happen to believe that there are a great deal of other documents that the OTP are aware of that are most certainly in their possession and that surely must be considered Rule 68 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us deal with this one first. It's Rule 68 documents. What are those four documents? I didn't follow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was four orders that we had that have already been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Orders. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So far. And I indicated to my learned friend this morning that a translation is ongoing. Documents are in the process of being translated now, and once they are translated then we certainly would live up to our obligation. This morning, Defence counsel indicated to us that she didn't mind receiving the documents in B/C/S, but that was only this morning. Hence the reason why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like to take this opportunity to make sure that apart from that EDS, it is the obligation of the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence exculpatory material in their actual knowledge on an ongoing basis. Do you have any observation on this, Ms. Henry-Benjamin or Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, any documents that are in our actual knowledge which fall within the scope of Rule 68 will be disclosed. However, it's our position that by making entire collections of documents available to the Defence in EDS, that that would satisfy our obligation under Rule 68 such that the Defence would be in a position to conduct its own electronic searches of that material. Now, with respect to material that was, for example, tendered into evidence in the Hadzihasanovic case and which is obviously in the direct knowledge or actual knowledge of the Prosecution as being Rule 68, we will simply provide that material to the Defence. We will also very shortly be inviting the Defence to provide us with any search terms so that we can conduct additional Rule 68 searches with respect to collections of material that is not populated in the EDS system. And that, of course, would include Rule 70 material, among other things. So we will be engaged in ongoing discussions with the Defence, but it is clearly, Your Honour, our position that one of the benefits of EDS is that it permits the Defence to do their own searches, and they can search for their own material without having to engage the Prosecution in that process. And we will certainly disclose on an ongoing basis documents and material which are in our actual knowledge which we believe fall within the scope of Rule 68. But making entire collections, thousands and thousands and thousands of documents available to the Defence in EDS will satisfy, in our opinion, our respectful view, our obligations under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in addition to that, Defence is able to inspect or make a search of the documents in the possession of the Prosecution according to Rule 66(B).

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, having heard these, is there any specific measure you are seeking in relation to Rule 68?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. What I said a while ago, and I wish to repeat now with great clarity, is it's not sufficient for documents to be available on EDS. There are millions of documents in that particular database. If we are expected to search this database in order to track down Rule 68 documents specifically, then the OTP must give us specific coordinates as to which collections we should be searching in relation to Rule 68 documents. I would like the OTP to be ordered immediately to serve on us Rule -- any remaining Rule 68 documents that are in their possession. These documents stem from the state archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We would like to gain access to potentially exculpatory documents from the BH archives, especially from the military security service archive. It is extremely difficult to identify these documents given what the EDS looks like now. It's very difficult for us to track these documents down and to find specific categories under which they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My recommendation is that -- in relation to the remaining documents, as you had put it, which is not in the EDS, I don't see any problem. The Prosecution will disclose it as soon as they find it. And in relation to the difficulty in locating and searching through EDS, it may be a bit early to resolve every matter at this stage. So I would very much encourage to have conversation with the Prosecution and resolve the matter in that way. And then I will turn to the supporting material. Are you -- Ms. Vidovic, you mentioned that the materials you were served seem to be different from that had been seen by the confirming judge. What's the basis of that? Yes, perhaps Mr. Mundis can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be easiest for me to explain that. Your Honour may recall some previous documentation that the Prosecution submitted on this issue to the Trial Chamber. When this indictment was submitted for confirmation, it appears as though the Prosecution inadvertently, when producing the supporting material, among the supporting material were a number of documents which had been printed using the double-sided feature of the computer printing. When those documents were then run through a photocopier, a number of pages were inadvertently not submitted to the confirming judge as part of the confirmation process. At the time when we discovered this, following the confirmation of the indictment, when preparing this supporting material for the benefit of the Accused, who at that time, as Your Honour is well aware, was not represented by counsel, the Prosecution in disclosing the material explained this to General Delic. And in order to provide him with the fullest possible set of documentation, we provided General Delic with a complete set of the -- what we had intended to submit to the supporting -- to the confirming judge, that is, we inserted the pages which had been missing when it was submitted for confirmation due to a photocopying error. In addition, we supplied him with a table indicating precisely which pages Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we inserted and the page numbers based on the Registry pagination system whereby those pages would be found. So that we explained to him that there were a number of pages that we had intended the supporting -- to go with the supporting material but which had not gone with the supporting material. We inserted those pages so that the Accused and now counsel would have the documents as we intended them to be, and we fully informed him which pages, in fact, were missing. So what we have is a situation where the Accused and as of today counsel have been provided with the supporting material that was provided to the confirming judge, but in addition to that, the pages which had inadvertently not been photocopied and submitted at the time the indictment was sent to the Registry for confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, my impression is that the part that Defence is concerned about is not related to that matter. Is there any redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that it is, in fact, that very issue, Your Honour, that, in effect, the issue that my learned colleague has raised is that we have provided them with more actual pages than were submitted to the confirming judge. If I'm mistaken in what she's -- the issue she's raising, I would be happy to be corrected, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, does the Prosecution's response resolve your concern?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand what the Prosecutor has just said. However, those are not my concerns. I'm concerned about the fact that voluminous material is concerned. I don't know whether you have had the opportunity of seeing the material but there is a lot of material from about 20 testimonies, and in each testimony, when the judge was confirming the indictment, the judge didn't see four, five, six or seven pages, and this is of extreme concern to me. I received this material this morning, and I find this very odd. I still don't know why this was done, and I believe that I have to analyse this issue very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand. That's a different matter from disclosure. So if there is a problem, you can raise it another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't believe this is the proper place to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted what I had said with regard to the material to be entered into the record because at the moment I don't really know what the significance of this is. That's all I would like to say. Perhaps certain problems will arise at a subsequent date and then I might want to return to the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see what we can do when the issue will arise. One thing I would like to raise is the issue of agreed facts. That's my preference as a Pre-Trial Judge, is to recommend the Prosecution to send, raise questions or a list of proposed facts for agreement to the Defence and then for the Defence to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, precisely what you said, but, in fact, counsel was just appointed, hence the reason why it not taken place as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And then I'm going to deal with some redaction in the indictment. I'd like to ask Mr. Mundis if I don't deal -- name the actual names, we can deal with it in public session. Yes. The original indictment included the names of some victims of rape, and the Prosecution filed a motion to redact those names in the public version, and the Chamber granted it. But I must say, it must have been by oversight on the part of the Prosecution and the Chamber; it was filed ex parte. Was there any reason for ex parte?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, or Your Honour, it was simply an oversight that perhaps slipped by due to taking an overly cautious approach with respect to the subject matter, but there is, in our respectful view, no need for that to remain ex parte; certainly confidential, but not ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I have to apologise to the Defence that Defence was not properly informed, but there will be no harm in it. All changed is that replacement of names into pseudonyms. And the effect of the decision would be, there would be public version of the indictment and the unredacted version, which should remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Defence is under obligation not to disclose the names of the victims of rape. Having said that, is there any matter to raise from the Defence in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have spoken about this matter to my client, and my client accepts the explanation provided with regard to the first indictment and in relation to the second indictment, so there is nothing that I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I dealt with all the agenda items I noted down. I wonder if there is any matter for the parties to raise. None from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is just one issue I would like to raise. I read the record of the 65 ter meeting, and the length of the trial was discussed, rather, the length of the Prosecution's case was discussed, and this also concerns the length of the entire trial. I have had some bad experience in the Oric case because of an erroneous estimate of the length of the time the trial would take. And this erroneous estimate in the Oric case, the Prosecutor 's erroneous estimate of the length that the Prosecution case -- of the time that the Prosecution case would last put us in a very difficult situation. I wouldn't like this to be repeated. So when my colleague is estimating how long the trial would length, I would be grateful if they could take the following into consideration: If they believe that 50 to 60 witnesses will be called, then it would be quite realistic to expect that we will need the same amount of time for our cross-examination as the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief. And in some cases, we'll need even more time. And during the Defence case, given the specific nature of this case, our client was the commander of the ABiH and is charged with crimes that occurred in the course of the conflict with the HVO, and the Republika Srpska army and foreign combatants are also involved, so it's very complex matter. And given all these factors, we believe that the Prosecutor's estimate with regard to the length of the trial is not realistic. Our client has the right to a fair trial, and we have the right to be allocated sufficient time for cross-examination and to present our evidence in order to ensure that the trial is fair. So I don't believe that the estimate is correct. In the Oric case the estimate was the trial would last for four months or, rather, the Prosecution case would last four months and in the end, it took them 8 and a half months to complete their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution must have heard that. And as for length of time and number of witnesses for this case, it may be a bit too early, so why don't you deal with it at next status conference, after having the 66(2) disclosure be completed, and we will have a -- may have the leave to amend the indictment by that time. So we can deal with that matter, including the matter of pre-trial brief et cetera. As for the estimation of length of time in Oric case, the fault may have been on me, as well, as the Pre-Trial Judge for that case. So let's try our best to have an exact anticipation of length of time in this case. So unless there are any other matters to be raised. Excuse me. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will let the parties know the next date for status conference in due course. It may be around -- from four months time from now, so it's about -- it's mid-October. The hearing is now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.15 p.m.
